subject: frontend
question: Does the .help-text colour meet WCAG AA contrast for normal-size text?
ai_claim: Yes. #999999 is a medium grey that is clearly readable on white, so it meets the AA requirement.

ai_solution.text: WCAG AA requires sufficient contrast between text and background.
Mid-grey on white is comfortably readable.

failure.misconception: Judging contrast by eye instead of by ratio
failure.explanation: WCAG AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text (14px is not large text). #999999 on #ffffff has a ratio of about 2.85:1, well short. Readability 'on my screen' is not the criterion; people with low vision and bright-light conditions are. #767676 is the lightest grey that reaches 4.5:1 on white.
failure.why_convincing: On a good monitor, in a dim room, the grey does look readable.

canonical_solution: No: the ratio is about 2.85:1, below the 4.5:1 required. Use #767676 or darker.

valid_evidence.summary: WCAG 1.4.3: normal text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.
A contrast checker reports 2.85:1 for #999999 on #ffffff.

hints.text: Contrast is measured, not judged.
Step 3 relies on how the colour looks.
AA for normal text requires a ratio of 4.5:1, computed from relative luminance.
Run the two colours through a contrast checker.
Step 3 is wrong: the ratio is 2.85:1, below 4.5:1. Use #767676 or darker.

repair: Darken the text to #767676 or darker.
debrief: Accessibility criteria are measurable, which is their strength: contrast is a ratio, not an opinion. Use the checker in DevTools or Lighthouse instead of judging on your own display.

subject: frontend
question: Is the AI right that this test would also fail if the Save button lost its accessible name - for example, if it became an icon-only button with no label?
ai_claim: Yes. getByRole finds elements the way assistive technology does. If the button no longer has the accessible name 'Save', the query throws and the test fails, which catches an accessibility regression.

ai_solution.text: getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }) searches the accessibility tree.
It matches only a button whose computed accessible name is 'Save'.
An icon-only button without a label has no such name.
So the query throws and the test fails.

canonical_solution: Correct. Role-and-name queries test the accessible interface. A getByTestId query would still pass on an unlabelled icon button.

valid_evidence.summary: Replace the button text with an <svg> and no aria-label: getByRole throws 'Unable to find an accessible element with the role "button" and name "Save"'.
getByTestId('save-btn') would keep passing after the label is removed.

hints.text: Check what getByRole's name option matches.
Step 2 depends on the computed accessible name.
Testing Library's role queries use the same role and name that screen readers expose.
Remove the button's text and run the test.
This solution is correct. Role-and-name queries fail when the accessible name disappears. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Tests written against roles and accessible names double as accessibility checks. Queries by test id or CSS class verify the DOM, not what users - including screen reader users - can find.

subject: frontend
question: Is it correct that only one request is sent, for 'lamp'?
ai_claim: Yes. Each keystroke restarts the 300 ms timer. The gaps are only about 80 ms, so the timer fires once, 300 ms after the last key, with 'lamp'.

ai_solution.text: debounce delays the call until 300 ms have passed with no new input.
Every keystroke within 300 ms cancels the pending call and restarts the timer.
The user pauses only after typing 'p'.
So one request for 'lamp' is sent.

canonical_solution: Correct. With a trailing debounce and gaps shorter than the delay, only the final value triggers a request - one call instead of four.

valid_evidence.summary: Typing 'lamp' with 80 ms gaps shows one request in the network panel, q=lamp.

hints.text: Compare the typing gaps with the debounce delay.
Step 2 says each keystroke restarts the timer.
A trailing debounce fires once the input has been quiet for the full delay.
Trace the timer across the four keystrokes.
This solution is correct. The 80 ms gaps keep resetting the 300 ms timer, so only 'lamp' is requested. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Debouncing trades a little latency for far fewer requests. It does not fix out-of-order responses on its own, so pair it with request cancellation for search-as-you-type.

subject: frontend
question: Did the analytics script cause the performance score to drop?
ai_claim: Yes. The commit only added the analytics script, and the score fell from 92 to 78, so the script caused the drop.

ai_solution.text: The commit's only change is the analytics script.
The score was 92 before the commit and 78 after.
Nothing else changed between the runs.
So the script caused the 14-point drop.

missing_information: Whether the difference is real or noise. With one run on each side, run-to-run variance (network, CPU load, throttling, extensions, third-party response times) can move Lighthouse scores by this much. We also do not know that the test conditions were identical.
resolving_scenarios: Five runs each give 90-93 before and 76-80 after, under the same conditions: the script very likely caused the drop.
Repeated runs of the new commit vary between 77 and 92: the single 78 was largely noise.
canonical_solution: A single run on each side cannot separate the change's effect from variance. Step 3 assumes identical conditions and no noise. Run each version several times under fixed conditions (or compare traces) before attributing the drop.

valid_evidence.summary: Re-running the 'after' commit could score 91, which would make the 78 an outlier.

counterexamples: Repeated runs of the same commit can differ by more than 10 points.

hints.text: Check how many measurements the conclusion rests on.
Step 3 assumes nothing else changed between the runs.
Lab performance scores vary between runs; one sample per side cannot establish a cause.
Ask what repeated runs of each version would show.
Step 3 assumes no noise. Consistent repeated runs would support the claim; noisy ones would not. It cannot be decided from one run each.

repair: Run Lighthouse several times per version under the same conditions and compare medians (or inspect the trace for the script's cost).
debrief: Performance measurements are noisy, so a before/after pair is an anecdote, not evidence. Attribute regressions with repeated runs, medians and traces - and the script may still be guilty, which is why this is undecided rather than flawed.
